text: inhibitor alone has also been used, allowing for complete corticosteroid withdrawal or avoidance.10 A review of corticosteroid-free strategies in liver trans- plantation concluded that up to 50% of patients can avoid corticosteroids with little modification of their mainte- nance immunosuppressive regimen; adding mycopheno- late mofetil and/or induction therapy with antibodies can increase this percentage, although over-immunosuppres- sion may be a problem. Although data are weak and limit- ed, corticosteroid avoidance is not advised with cal- cineurin inhibitor monotherapy, nor with calcineurin inhibitors and azathioprine; it may be feasible with tac- rolimus and mycophenolate mofetil, or with calcineurin inhibitors and antibodies. Benefits of corticosteroid avoid- ance are seen in growth rates in children, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, CMV infection, and possibly other infec- tions.11 Patients with underlying auto-immune hepatitis or inflammatory bowel disease may be relatively refractory to corticosteroid withdrawal.12 Tacrolimus is better than ciclosporin at preventing acute rejection in liver transplantation. It is also marginally bet- ter at preventing patient death and graft loss, but it increas- es the risk of post-transplant diabetes.13 Studies of differ- ent formulations of ciclosporin found a reduced incidence of rejection with the microemulsifying formulation com- pared with the older oil-based product.5 The use of azathioprine in liver transplant patients has been limited due to its possible hepatotoxicity.10 Myco- phenolate mofetil has been used in place of azathioprine, to reduce the dose of the calcineurin inhibitor or corticos- teroid used, and possibly prevent rejection.2,8 Calcineurin inhibitors have been replaced with mycophenolate mofetil in an attempt to improve renal function,10 although a small study has suggested that this monotherapy carries a high risk of rejection.14 The long-term efficacy of calcineurin inhibitor minimisation or avoidance has yet to be deter- mined.15 The role of sirolimus in liver transplantation has yet to be evaluated.3 There have been reports of efficacy when used with a calcineurin inhibitor,1,9 which might al- low dose reduction9 or withdrawal of therapy5 in patients with toxicity from tacrolimus or ciclosporin, but excess mortality, graft loss, and hepatic artery thrombosis has been associated with such use.
